planting.note: Nick or soak the hard-coated seed before sowing directly into lean, well-drained soil; plants form a dense root system in year one and flower from the second year onward.

directions: Ononis spinosa is a wiry, spine-tipped European legume subshrub of dry chalk grassland and roadside verges, named for its tenacious, tough taproots that were said to catch and stop a horse-drawn harrow. Small pink pea flowers appear along the spiny stems in mid to late summer, followed by small pods, and the plant fixes its own nitrogen, thriving in poor, lean, unamended ground. The dried root bark has a long folk history as a mild diuretic used for gravel and minor urinary complaints. Grow in full sun on sharply drained, even gravelly, low-fertility soil; rich or damp ground produces lank, floppy growth and shortens the plant's lifespan.

planting.note: Direct-sow into sharply drained, gritty soil after the last frost; in colder zones grow as an annual or overwinter potted specimens under cover.

directions: Anacyclus pyrethrum forms a low, feathery-leaved mat of finely divided foliage topped with chamomile-like daisy flowers whose petals are white above and deep maroon-red beneath. It is not the same plant as insecticidal pyrethrum (Tanacetum cinerariifolium) despite the shared common name; the pungency here comes from the root, which contains a numbing, saliva-stimulating compound that has made it a classic Mediterranean and North African remedy chewed fresh or dried to relieve toothache and dry mouth. Plant in gritty, low-fertility, sharply drained soil in full sun; standing winter wet is the most common cause of failure. Harvest roots from established two-year-old plants in autumn for drying.

planting.note: Divide the spreading rhizome in early spring and replant sections 2-3 inches deep in cool, humus-rich soil; established clumps naturalize readily in alpine and subalpine meadow conditions.

directions: Not to be confused with the unrelated ornamental Astrantia major, which shares the English name masterwort, Peucedanum ostruthium (formerly classed as Imperatoria ostruthium) is a robust Apiaceae relative of angelica and lovage native to the mountain meadows and pastures of central and southern Europe. It produces broad, deeply divided leaves and flat umbels of small white flowers atop hollow stems, with a pungently aromatic rhizome long chewed or infused by alpine herders as a digestive bitter and traditionally credited with easing the effects of high-altitude exertion. Its dried root remains a flavoring component in some traditional European herbal bitters and mountain liqueurs. Grow in cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to light sun; plants resent hot, dry summers and perform best in climates that mimic their subalpine origin. Divide congested clumps every 3-4 years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or softwood cuttings after last frost; Roman wormwood spreads by shallow rhizomes and is almost always propagated vegetatively rather than from seed.

directions: Native to southeastern Europe, Artemisia pontica forms a low, finely cut, silver-gray colony of aromatic foliage that is markedly less bitter than common wormwood, making it prized historically as a gentler flavoring herb in the production of vermouth and certain herbal bitters and cordials. Its old English name Roman wormwood distinguishes it from both true wormwood and mugwort. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, where it spreads slowly by rhizome to form an attractive weed-suppressing patch; rich, damp soil causes floppy, sprawling growth. Shear plants back hard in early spring to keep the silvery foliage dense and prevent the clump from thinning at the center.

planting.note: Plant divisions of the creeping rhizome into consistently moist to wet soil in spring; this rhizomatous spreader is best sited where its running roots can be contained, such as a bog garden edge or large container.

directions: Stachys palustris is a circumboreal mint-family perennial of wet meadows, ditch banks, and pond margins, bearing soft, hairy, nettle-shaped leaves (without any sting) and whorled spikes of dusky pink-purple flowers through summer. Old herbals rank fresh-crushed marsh woundwort leaves among the most effective traditional first-aid poultices for stopping bleeding and speeding the healing of cuts and wounds, a reputation some herbalists held in even higher regard than betony. The slender, knobby white tubers are edible and related in flavor to the cultivated Chinese artichoke, though smaller and more fibrous. Plant in reliably moist to wet, full-sun soil; the running rhizomes spread readily in favorable conditions, so give it room or a barrier in smaller gardens.

planting.note: Plant divisions of the creeping mat into lean, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in early spring; established patches root along their trailing stems and spread readily.

directions: Veronica officinalis forms a low, ground-hugging mat of hairy, oval, scalloped leaves on trailing stems that root as they spread, sending up short spikes of small pale-blue to lilac flowers with darker veining in early summer. Native to dry heaths, moors, and open woodland across Europe, it was once dried and steeped as a substitute for imported tea, giving rise to the old name European tea, and used in folk medicine for coughs, catarrh, and minor skin irritations. Grow in lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade; overly rich or wet ground encourages rot and weakens the tight, mat-forming habit. Trim lightly after flowering to keep growth dense and encourage fresh rooting along the stems.
